client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Margaret. I'm Dr. Chen. Before we get started I want to be upfront about how I work — I'm going to ask questions and mostly listen. Nothing gets decided today without you being part of it. There's no agenda I'm pushing. Does that sound alright?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sure, that's... that's fine. I'll be honest with you, I've done this before — the counseling thing — and it hasn't really gone anywhere. But my doctor seemed to think it was important, so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been through counseling before and it hasn't felt useful — and you came anyway. I want to hear about what's been going on lately, in your own words. Not what your doctor wrote down. Just what life has looked like for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, um... I have a lot of pain. Arthritis, mostly, hips and lower back. Been dealing with it for about ten years now. And somewhere along the way I started having a glass of wine before bed to help with the sleep. And then it became two, and then sometimes during the day if the pain was particularly bad. I don't know. It doesn't feel like a... a big problem to me. But I know that's why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it started as something practical. You were in real pain, you needed sleep, and the wine helped. That makes sense.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. The medication only does so much. My doctor keeps adjusting things but honestly... I'm not going to lie, the wine works faster. My children are worried though. My daughter especially — she called my doctor, which is how all this started. I don't want to make a fuss. I really don't want to be a burden to anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you make of your daughter reaching out to your doctor the way she did?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, she means well. She really does. I suppose she saw something that concerned her. When she visited in February she said I seemed... foggy. That was the word she used. Foggy. I didn't like hearing that. But I also thought — it was a terrible week for pain. Anyone would've seemed foggy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That word stuck with you. Even if part of you pushed back on it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I think it did. I've always been sharp — I was a school librarian for thirty-two years. I prided myself on that, being organized, clear-headed. So that word. That wasn't easy to hear.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about the pain at night. What is it actually like, and what happens on the nights when the wine isn't enough?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... it's relentless. It just doesn't go away. And when I'm lying there and I can't get comfortable I think, well, if I have another glass maybe my body will just let me sleep. Sometimes it works. Sometimes I'm still up at three in the morning anyway and I feel... defeated. And I know I should worry about the medication on top of it, but the pain is so real and right there, and the worry feels more... abstract, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I've heard. You've been managing serious, ongoing pain for years, and the drinking started as a solution — something practical that helped you function and sleep. But there are things that have started to concern you: your daughter's worry, that word 'foggy,' the nights where the wine isn't even enough anymore. And underneath all of it is this thing you care about deeply — not being a burden, and not losing the sharpness that's always been part of who you are. Does that capture it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yes. Yes, that's it. I hadn't quite put it together like that. The sharp part — that does matter to me. A lot. I've always managed things on my own. I don't like asking for help. But I don't want my grandchildren to see me... not as myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to you to still be yourself — clear-headed, present — ten years from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd want to still be able to have a real conversation. To remember things. My oldest grandson, he's eight, and he asks me all sorts of questions — about history, about books — and I want to be able to answer him. I want to be present for that. I know that sounds like I'm already assuming the worst, but... I do think about it. More than I let on.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being present for him — answering his questions, being the grandmother who's really there — that's not a small thing. That's everything. And the fact that you came today, even after counseling hasn't worked before, tells me you haven't given up on that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. I haven't. I think I've been waiting for someone to give me a reason that felt real. My daughter talks about my health like it's a checklist. But my grandson... yes. That feels real. Maybe I've been thinking about this the wrong way. Maybe I can do something about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned past counseling felt like it went nowhere. Knowing what you know now — given everything you've just shared — what do you think would need to be different this time for it to actually help you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think I need someone to talk about the pain, not just the drinking. They always treated those as separate things. But they're not, are they? If we could actually work on something real for the pain — real options, not just telling me to use a heating pad — I think I might actually be able to change something. I'm willing to try. I really am.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm glad you made it. Before we get into anything, I just want to hear from you — what's your sense of why you're here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor basically told me I had to come. Something about my blood work. I'll be honest with you, I think it's a whole lot of nothing. I've been working construction for twenty years, my liver's fine, I feel fine. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're here because someone else thought you should be, not because you woke up this morning thinking you needed this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Look, I got up at four-thirty, I put in a full day on a jobsite, and now I'm sitting here. No offense. I just... I don't see what the big deal is. Guys I work with drink way more than me. This is just how it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What exactly did your doctor tell you about the bloodwork? Like, what were the actual words he used?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He said my liver enzymes were elevated. AST, ALT, something like that. And that the numbers were — I don't know — twice what they should be? He started talking about fatty liver, possible scarring... I kind of tuned him out after a while. He always overdoes it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You heard it, took it in, and your gut said — that's not me, my doctor's being dramatic. That's a pretty strong reaction. It tells me you've got a clear picture of yourself, who you are, what you can handle.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I've been doing this — the drinking, the work, the whole thing — same routine for like fifteen years. Nothing's changed. I'm not falling down, I'm not missing work. My wife doesn't say anything. So I don't know what everyone's so worked up about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to be straight with you, because I get the sense you'd rather have that than me dancing around it. Liver damage from alcohol is different from most things — it doesn't give you a lot of warning signs. You can feel totally fine, totally functional, and those enzymes are quietly telling a different story. Twice the normal level isn't nothing. That's your liver working harder than it should to keep you upright.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Okay. I mean. I hear you. But lots of things can cause that, right? Like, stress, or... I don't know, diet? I eat like crap on the jobsite. Could be that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Sure, other things can contribute. What's your honest read on it, though? When you factor in a six-pack every night — what do you think is most likely driving those numbers?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... probably the drinking. I'm not stupid. I just — I don't know. It's not like I'm drinking vodka for breakfast. It's beer. After work. It's how I decompress, you know? I've got a stressful job. I come home, I have a few beers, I watch the game, I go to bed. That's it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes sense. It works for you — helps you shift gears, come down from the day. And at the same time, part of you just said 'probably the drinking.' You know something's there, even if you're not sure what to do with it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I guess. It's just — I've never had to think about it before, you know? It's always just been a thing I do. It's not like I sit there and crave it or whatever. I just... it's routine. But if my liver's actually messed up, that's... I don't know. That's different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it actually mean for you — practically, day to day — if your liver got worse? What's at stake for you personally?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I got two kids. Fourteen and sixteen. And my job — I can't do what I do if I'm sick. Like, construction, you need to be on. You can't be dragging yourself around a site with liver problems. My guys count on me. And my wife... she'd lose her mind if something happened to me. She already worries too much as it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're someone people depend on — your crew, your kids, your wife. That's not a small thing. And you're sitting here putting that up against what the bloodwork is telling you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, when you put it like that... I'm not trying to check out early. My dad died at fifty-eight, heart stuff, and I always swore I wouldn't do that to my kids. I just never connected the drinking to — I don't know. Any of that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So here's where I'm hearing you land — you came in skeptical, figured your doctor was making a mountain out of a molehill. But the numbers are real, and somewhere in there, you know the drinking is probably connected. You're not someone who falls apart, you pull your weight, you show up. And you've got people counting on you to keep doing that. You haven't decided anything yet, and I'm not asking you to. But something shifted a little today, I think.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Maybe. I'm not making any promises. But I'll think about it. I'll actually think about it this time.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again, Marcus. Before we get into anything structured, I just want to check in — how's the week been since we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: How's the week been. Are you serious right now. I gotta drive forty-five minutes each way to sit in this chair and answer that question. The week's been garbage, same as every week. You know what, I'm only here because the court says I have to be. Let's just be real about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You didn't want to be here today. That comes through loud and clear. And you've made that drive, sat down, showed up anyway — even with all of that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah well, I don't exactly have a choice, do I. Judge Whoever gets to decide how I spend my Thursday afternoons now. Second DUI, suddenly I'm some kind of... I don't know, criminal. Like I didn't just make a mistake. Two mistakes. Whatever. The system's designed to grind people down and that's exactly what it's doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It feels like something's been taken from you — your time, your autonomy, your sense of being treated fairly. That's a real loss. I also remember you mentioned last time that things at home were... tense. I'm wondering how that's been sitting with you this week.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Tense. Yeah, that's one word for it. Dana's... she said some things last weekend that I can't really... look, she's not wrong to be upset. I get it. I just — I don't know how to fix something when everybody's coming at me from every direction at the same time. I had a few drinks last Saturday. That's why I'm bringing it up, I guess. Before you ask.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You brought that up yourself. That took something. So Dana said some things last weekend — and you're still carrying that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said she doesn't know if she can do this anymore. The marriage. She said she's been watching me for two years just... waiting for things to get better and they keep not getting better. And the thing is... she's not wrong. I know she's not wrong. I just — when she says it out loud like that it just... I shut down. I don't know what to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When she put it that plainly, it landed differently than usual. I want to ask you something, and take your time with it — what is it that you actually don't want to lose here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My kids. My... I mean Dana too, obviously. But my kids most of all. Tyler's eleven and he already looks at me different. Like he's — I don't know, like he's waiting for me to screw up. And I'm doing it. I'm giving him exactly what he's waiting for. That's... yeah. That's what I don't want to lose.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You came in angry today — about the drive, the court, the whole setup. And underneath that, there's a father who's watching his eleven-year-old son pull away from him. A husband who heard his wife say she's close to done. And somewhere in the middle of all that pressure last Saturday, you drank. Not because you don't care — but maybe because you do, and it's overwhelming.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I mean. When you say it like that it sounds... yeah. I don't think of myself as someone who can't handle things. I used to be the person who handled things. I was reliable. I don't know when that changed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You described a rough patch this week — and part of that was drinking on Saturday. Walk me through what that day actually looked like, if you're willing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... I don't know, stupid, looking back. Dana and I had an argument in the morning, nothing huge, but she got quiet on me. The silence is worse than the yelling, I think. And I'm just sitting there in the garage and I'm thinking about the court dates and the fines and Tyler not wanting to play catch anymore and I just — I grabbed a beer. Then another one. By the time I stopped I'd had like six. I didn't go anywhere. I wasn't driving. But I know that's not... that's not the point.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You knew it wasn't the point even while it was happening. That awareness — that's not nothing, Marcus. A lot of people don't have that. You're watching yourself and you don't like what you see. That's actually a kind of honesty that's hard to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been doing that my whole life though. Watching myself make the wrong call and doing it anyway. It's like I know the answer and I still pick wrong. I'm thirty-eight years old. At what point does that stop being something I can blame on stress or a bad week.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a genuinely important question you just asked yourself. So I want to turn it back to you — not in a gotcha way, but honestly — what would it look like, for you, to start picking differently?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... being present, maybe. Like actually in the room with my kids instead of just in the house. Not using a beer to turn the volume down on everything. I don't — I'm not saying I'm an alcoholic or whatever label we're supposed to use. But I can see that it's become like a... a default. And that scares me a little. That it's a default.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to hold what you just said, because you've covered a lot of ground today. You came in ready to fight the whole process. And by the end of it, you're sitting here naming your own pattern — calling it a default, saying it scares you, talking about what being present for Tyler could actually mean. You didn't have to go there. You went there anyway. Whatever we work on next, that's the foundation.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I don't know if I'm ready to like, commit to anything. But I'll think about what you said. About the volume thing. I think that's actually — yeah. I think that's real. I'll think about it.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, Marcus — do you mind if I call you that? Your chart says you were encouraged to come in. I'm curious what that looked like from your side — what's been going on for you lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, Marcus is fine. Um... I mean, my wife basically said she'd leave if I didn't come. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She drew a line.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Which... I get it, I guess. She's been watching me just — disappear into work and the drinking, and I think she's scared. I'm not totally blind to that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's it actually been like these past few months — for you, on the inside of all of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Kind of a blur. My thesis committee basically told me my last chapter draft was... not up to standard. And my advisor pulled me aside after a group meeting and said my work has been 'inconsistent.' Which is his polite way of saying it's gotten worse. I don't know, I just... I started having a couple beers to unwind at night and it kind of became more than a couple. I didn't really notice when that happened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That feedback from your advisor hit hard. And the drinking started as a way to get through it — to get some relief from something that sounds genuinely painful.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, like... I'm surrounded by people who just seem to have it figured out, you know? They're publishing, networking, whatever. And I'm sitting there wondering if I even belong in the program at all. The beer just — it quiets that noise. For a little while at least. I know that's not, like, a great reason but it works.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That feeling of not belonging — that's doing a lot of work on you. How much are you actually drinking on a typical night right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: More than I should. I don't know, like... six, seven drinks some nights. More on weekends sometimes. I didn't even realize the full picture until my wife started keeping track and she showed me this list and I was just like... oh. Okay. That's a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Seeing it written down like that — the actual number — something shifted when she showed you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... yeah. Hard to argue with a list. And she wasn't yelling at me. She was just quiet. That was worse somehow. She looked tired.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to ask you something a little different, and take your time with it. When you imagine actually finishing this PhD — walking out with that degree — what does that mean to you? Not what it means to your program. To you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... everything. My parents came here from Gujarat with basically nothing. My dad worked in a factory his whole life. Nobody in my family has a PhD. Nobody even has a graduate degree. I just — I always wanted to be the person who proved that it was possible. For them. For... I don't know. It sounds really cheesy saying it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not cheesy. That's exactly why you're still in the program when it would have been a lot easier to quit. You've kept going through imposter syndrome, a rough review from your committee, your marriage under strain. That takes something real.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never... huh. I never thought about it that way. I just always feel like I'm barely hanging on. But I guess — yeah. I haven't quit. I keep showing up even when it's bad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me try to pull this together. You came in because your wife reached her limit — but sitting here, you've told me that your advisor has noticed a drop in your work, your committee gave you hard feedback, and six or seven drinks a night has become your way of managing the voice that says you don't belong. And underneath all of it is this degree that means everything — for your parents, for yourself. The thing you're using to cope is quietly eating away at the thing that matters most to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... yeah. That's exactly it. Like, the drinking is supposed to help me cope with feeling like a fraud, but it's actually the reason my work is slipping, which just makes me feel more like a fraud. It's this loop I can't get out of. I've kind of known that but I hadn't, like, said it out loud before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just named that loop yourself — clearly, on your own. That matters more than you think. So let me ask: what's one small thing, even something tiny, that you could try this week? Not to fix everything. Just one step that points slightly outside that loop.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... okay, maybe not drinking on the nights I'm supposed to be writing. Because honestly I've been using it to, like, get started, and it doesn't even work — I just end up on Reddit for two hours. Maybe those nights I just make tea or go for a walk first and see what happens. I think I could actually try that.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to start by just... acknowledging that you're here. That's not a small thing — finishing a detox program and then walking into a room like this, first session, not knowing what to expect. That takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah well. My doctor said I had to come so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Here you are. ... And I'm wondering — what's it like, sitting here right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Feels like a waste of time. No offense. I did the detox, I checked the box, I don't — look, I've been drinking since I was like nineteen. Guys I served with, everybody drinks. That's just... that's the culture. It's not like I have some kind of disease.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That culture — the drinking being woven into everything, the way it binds people together — that's real. I don't want to dismiss that. ... So I guess I'm curious, if it's always been normal, always been just part of the life... what made you actually go through with the detox?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife. She, um... she said she was done. Like done done. Had her bags kind of... she didn't leave but it felt like she was about to. And I — I don't know, I just. I couldn't let that happen.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She was at the door. And something in you said — not this. Not her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I guess. I love her. We've been together since before I deployed the second time, she's — she stuck around through a lot of shit, excuse my language. And I kept telling myself it wasn't that bad, you know? Like I'm functioning, I'm not passed out in a ditch somewhere. But she said... she said she doesn't recognize me anymore. And that kind of... that one got in there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: "She doesn't recognize me anymore." ... That landed somewhere deep.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. ... Because I don't — I'm not even sure I recognize myself either. Like the guy I was before the second tour, that guy was — I don't know where he went. And somewhere in between all of it I just started drinking more and it kind of... filled something. I don't know. That sounds stupid.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound stupid at all. It sounds like you lost someone — yourself — and the drinking was a way to not feel that loss so much. ... Can I ask — when you think about your wife, about maybe losing her — what comes up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Terror. I mean — I'm not supposed to say that, right, I'm supposed to be tough or whatever. But yeah. It's terror. And we have a daughter. She's seven. And I catch her sometimes looking at me and I can tell she's — she's trying to figure out if I'm gonna be okay. A seven-year-old shouldn't have to do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A seven-year-old watching her dad, trying to read the room... ... You noticed that. You let yourself see it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's hard to. It's easier to just... not look. But then you said something about — I don't know. Not feeling the loss. And I keep thinking about that. Because I've been not looking for a long time and it hasn't — it hasn't actually helped anything. My daughter's still watching me. My wife's still half out the door. So. Maybe not looking hasn't been working so great.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's this real tension you're describing — drinking felt like it was holding something together, something painful from the deployments, and at the same time it's been quietly pulling apart the things that matter most to you. Your wife. Your daughter. Yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. ... Yeah, that's — that's pretty much it. I kept thinking it was helping me hold it together. But I think I was just holding it together enough to keep drinking. Which is not the same thing. At all.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think you've said some really significant things today. You came in here feeling like this was a box to check — understandable, you didn't choose this. But when you started talking about your wife, something shifted. You told me she said she doesn't recognize you, and that you don't recognize yourself either. That there's a version of you from before that's missing. And that your seven-year-old daughter is carrying something she shouldn't have to carry. And underneath all of it, there's this part of you — the part that showed up today — that isn't willing to let this be the end of the story.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah, I — when you say it like that. I'm tired of losing things. I'm tired of it. I survived two tours, I'm not gonna — I don't want to lose my family sitting in my own living room. That's not how this ends.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not how this ends. ... I want to hold onto that. What does it look like — even just a small piece of it — if things start moving in the right direction? What's the first thing you'd want to be different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want my daughter to stop watching me like that. I want her to just — be a kid. And I want my wife to look at me the way she used to. I don't know if that's possible yet but I... I think I want to find out. That's maybe the most honest thing I've said in a long time.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you. So you mentioned things got a little rocky this past week — what's been going on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know. It's not really that big a deal. My friends are being way too dramatic about everything. I came back from spring break and everyone's acting like I killed somebody.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Coming home felt like walking straight into a wall.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. Like, we all went to Cancun together, right? And sure, some stuff happened, but that's just — that's what happens on spring break. I'm a college senior. This is literally the last spring break of my life and everyone wants to make it this whole thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What kind of stuff happened down there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... I blacked out a couple times. Which, okay, I know how that sounds. But it was spring break. And then apparently I — I don't even fully remember this — I called my mom at like 3am and she freaked out. And now my friends won't shut up about it, and my doctor is making me come in for check-ins, and I just feel like... everyone's watching me now. All the time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a lot of people suddenly paying very close attention to something you've always kind of felt was just... normal.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right? And this is going to sound bad, but it feels like everyone just decided overnight that I have a problem. When like — nothing changed. I didn't change. The same stuff I've always done is suddenly this huge crisis and I don't — I don't get it. It's like they all had a meeting without me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And underneath all that frustration with everyone's reaction... what do you notice when you sit with that 3am call to your mom?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... She cried. When I talked to her the next day, she actually cried. And I didn't — I genuinely don't remember making the call. Like at all. There's just nothing there. And I keep trying to piece it together and I can't. What did I even say to her?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not knowing what you said — that gap is sitting with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She wouldn't really tell me. Just kept saying I was 'really out of it' and that I was 'saying things.' I don't know what that means. And those hours just — they don't exist. Like, I've blacked out before, whatever, but... I don't know. This one felt different. She looked at me differently when I got home. My own mom.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing. Your friends came at you hard after break, you're feeling watched and judged on all sides — that part you're pretty clear about, and you can push back on it. But then there's this other thing. The call. The gaps. The way your mom looked at you. And those two things seem to be pulling at you in pretty different ways.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah, I guess. Like I can deal with my friends being overdramatic, that's easy. But my mom's not like that. She doesn't make things up. If she was crying, she was actually scared. And that makes me feel like maybe — God, I don't know — maybe I don't have the full picture of what happened out there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Some part of you is open to the idea that there might be more to see here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe. Like a one percent chance. I'm not saying I have a problem — I want to be really clear about that. But there's this tiny part of me that's like... okay, maybe this is worth thinking about. That's not the same as what everyone else is saying though. They want me to stop drinking completely? That's not realistic. That's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That one percent — what would it mean for you to follow that thread a little? Just that one percent.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess I'd want to actually understand what's happening. Like — is this a pattern or was spring break just spring break. Because I actually have plans, you know? I'm not trying to be the guy who peaked in college and is at rock bottom by 30. That's not the story I have for myself. So... yeah. I don't know. I'd want to know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know who you want to be. That matters to you — enough that even through all of this, even with every reason to just shut the door on it, you're still sitting here willing to look at it. Even if it's just one percent. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... I mean, I'm still not — I'm not saying I have a problem. I just want to be clear on that. But I guess I can... actually look at it instead of just defending myself every time someone brings it up. Maybe. I don't know. Maybe.

client_context: A 20-year-old star athlete whose performance has been slipping due to partying. Coach gave an ultimatum. Torn between team loyalty and social life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for coming in today. I know it's not always the easiest thing to... show up for something like this. I'm really glad you're here. So, maybe just start wherever feels right — what brings you in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... my friends basically made me come. Like, they cornered me after practice and said I needed to talk to someone. I don't — I mean, I'm fine. I just... I don't really know why I'm here, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it wasn't really your idea, and part of you isn't sure this is something you need. And yet... you came anyway.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. I guess. My buddy Marcus, he was — he looked really worried when he pulled me aside. I've never seen him like that before. So I figured, whatever, I'll just come in and then everyone can relax and get off my back.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Seeing Marcus like that — that landed differently than you expected. What do you think he was seeing that had him that worried?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, yeah, I've been going out more, but... it's college. Everyone does that, right? It's not like I'm — and then Coach pulled me aside last week and said if my times don't come up he's pulling me from the relay. Which is... I've been on the relay since freshman year. That's not... I don't know. That was a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That hit hard. The relay — that's not just a spot on a team. That's something you've been part of for years.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it really did. Like, swimming is... it's everything. My whole scholarship is tied to it. And my parents — we don't have money like that, so if I lose the scholarship... I can't even let myself think about that. It kind of makes me sick when I do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying a lot — the team, your scholarship, your family counting on you. That's real weight. And it takes honesty to say that out loud the way you just did. Can I ask — when you're out with your friends, what does that give you? What are you getting from those nights?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's the only time I'm not — swimming takes up everything. Every morning, every afternoon, there's always something I should be doing. When I'm out I can just be a regular person, you know? Not Jake the swimmer. Just Jake. And it's fun. Or it... it used to feel more fun. Lately it's kind of just like... I don't know. Habit, maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A chance to just be yourself. Not the athlete, not the guy the scholarship is riding on. Just... you. And you're noticing something's changed — it doesn't feel the same way it used to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. That's actually kind of exactly it. Like I started doing it to decompress or whatever, but now I wake up on Sundays feeling like garbage, my times are down, and I'm not even having that much fun anymore. I'm just going through the motions. Which is... I never said that out loud before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you picture where you want to be — say, a year from now — what does that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I want to make it to nationals. That's been the goal since... forever, basically. And I want to not have my parents stressed. My mom calls every Sunday and I've been kind of avoiding her because I don't want her to hear that things aren't going well. I hate that I've been doing that. That's not — that's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I'm understanding everything you've shared. You came in today because people who care about you were worried — Marcus, your coach. Part of you figured you'd come in and ease their minds. But as we've talked, something else has come up. You started going out to feel like yourself, to breathe a little, but now it's turned into something that's getting in the way — of your times, of nationals, of being honest with your mom. And that gap, between who you want to be and where things are heading right now... that actually matters to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...When you put it like that. Yeah. I mean, I've been telling myself it's not a big deal, but... it kind of is, isn't it. It's been adding up and I've just been looking the other way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for you to start looking at it... directly?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think I actually want to get back to where I was. Like, before this year. I felt good then. I was hitting times I was proud of and I wasn't avoiding my mom's calls. I want that feeling back. I didn't think I'd say that today, but... yeah. I think that's what I want.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not a small thing to recognize. You walked in here not really sure why you came, and you found something real — that what you want for yourself is bigger than the habit you've been caught in. You said it yourself: I want that feeling back. That's yours. That's something to build from.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I... yeah. I think I'm ready to actually — I don't know exactly what that looks like yet, but I want to figure it out. I don't want to be the guy who threw everything away because he couldn't get it together. That's not me. That's not who I want to be.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just came through five days of detox. That takes something out of a person. What was it that got you through the door today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My brother basically dragged me here. I don't... I mean, I knew I needed to do the detox thing, that part I get. I was shaking bad. But I don't really know what I'm supposed to do now, sitting here talking to — no offense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No offense taken. So the detox was necessary — your body made that pretty clear. And now you're here, not totally sure what this is supposed to accomplish.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Look, I'm not some — I wasn't always like this. Four months ago I had a house, I had my kids every other weekend, I had... and then Sandra just — sorry. I don't know why I'm saying all this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No, keep going. What happened four months ago?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She left. Twenty-two years and she just — she said she'd been unhappy for a long time. I didn't even see it coming, that's the thing. I just... I started drinking more, and then more, and I kept thinking I'd stop when I felt better. But I never felt better. So. Here we are.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years. That's not just a marriage ending — that's your entire life getting reorganized around something that's suddenly gone. And you still walked through detox. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't really feel like it's brave or whatever. I feel like... empty. Like what's the point. My kids are gonna grow up and their dad's gonna be the drunk guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That image — being 'the drunk guy' to your kids — that one lands differently than everything else you've said.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It terrifies me. Jake is fifteen, he's already pulling away, and... yeah. That's the part I can't live with. Everything else, maybe I deserve it. But not that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think it would take — for Jake, for that relationship — to not go down that road?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Showing up, I guess. Actually being... present. Not calling him when I've been drinking, which I've done, and I hate myself for it. Just being someone he doesn't have to be ashamed of. I haven't figured out how to do that yet but... I know that's what I want.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm hearing you right. You didn't plan for any of this — the divorce blindsided you, and drinking became the only way to get through the days. But what's been eating at you most isn't even the marriage ending. It's Jake. The thought of him looking at you a certain way. You came through detox, you're sitting here, and when you talk about him, something shifts. That's still alive in you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's right. I mean, I'm still angry at Sandra, I'm not gonna pretend I'm not. But Jake didn't do anything. He just has a dad who fell apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've got real anger, real grief, and a very clear reason to fight. What would it look like — three months from now — if things were moving in the right direction with Jake?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... showing up to his baseball games sober. Not just physically there but actually — he'd look over and see me and not have to worry. That'd be something. That'd be a start.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just described a very specific version of yourself — not perfect, just present and trustworthy. And you called it a start. That's a grounded way to think about this. Not all-or-nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I always thought I had to fix everything at once and then when I couldn't I'd just... give up. Maybe that's been part of it. Like, maybe I can just try to not drink today. And then tomorrow. I don't know, maybe that's actually — maybe that's possible.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So here's where you are: you came out of detox, you're not here because you have all the answers, you're here because of Jake. Because of who you want to be for him. There's real grief about the marriage, real anger, and underneath all of it — this clear picture of a dad who shows up. One day at a time isn't giving up on the bigger goal. It's how you get there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I think I can do that. I mean... I hope I can. But I actually — yeah. I want to try.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know finishing detox and then walking straight into this — that's a lot to navigate in a short amount of time. Before we get into anything, how are you doing right now, in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm okay. Just... tired. Really tired.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What feels most important to you to talk about today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I don't even know where to start. I know what I'm supposed to say — that I have a problem, that I need help. And I get it, okay, I do. But it's like... I was just trying to survive. Working those hours, what I was seeing every shift — anyone would've needed something. It wasn't like I was just, I don't know, drinking for fun.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were doing what you had to do to get through it. And for a while, it worked.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. But even saying that — I still feel like I'm being judged. Like all anyone sees now is the drinking. Not what I was going through. Not what I saw every single shift. People died alone, I held their hands, I called their families at 3 AM, and then I went home and... I mean, what was I supposed to do with all of that?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You carried an enormous amount for years and you kept showing up anyway. And then you completed detox — that's genuinely hard. A lot of people don't make it through.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I know. I just — I don't feel like it's something to be proud of. Like, I shouldn't have needed it in the first place. I'm a nurse. I know better. I knew better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What worries you most about what comes next — now that you're out?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I go back. That I walk into that ER and it's exactly the same — the chaos, the short staffing, someone coding at 2 AM — and I just... I don't have a plan. Everyone keeps saying find other coping strategies and I'm like, okay, I'm mid-trauma shift, what am I supposed to do, step outside for a breathing exercise? I don't know how to do this sober. I genuinely don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fear isn't just about wanting to drink — it's that you genuinely don't know how you'll get through those moments without it. Like the tool's gone and there's nothing in its place yet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And people keep saying it gets easier but they don't work my floor. They don't know. And look — there was this moment a few months back where I almost gave a patient the wrong medication. I caught it. But I was so foggy and run down, and... even that didn't fully stop me. What does that say about me? I was scared and I still kept going.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it say to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That I was losing control and I knew it. That I was becoming someone I... don't want to be. I used to be the nurse people came to when they were scared — new grads, families, even other staff. Like, she knows what to do, she stays calm. I was good at that. And now I'm — I'm the one who can't be trusted. That's hard to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It is hard. And you said it anyway. That nurse you're describing — the one people came to — she clearly still means a lot to you. That part of you didn't disappear.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. She didn't. And I think — I think that's actually why I went through with the detox. Because I could feel myself disappearing and I didn't want to lose her completely. There's still something in me that's... fighting for that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I can pull together what I'm hearing. You went through years of real sustained trauma — pandemic shifts, people dying, holding it together for everyone else — and alcohol became the thing that made it survivable. You knew something was wrong, a near-miss with a patient made that undeniable, and still it took everything you had to get through detox. And underneath all of it, there's still this nurse who cares deeply about her patients and her team — who wants to be sharp and present and someone people can count on. That part never left. And maybe that's what got you here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's right. I mean, I'm still scared. I won't pretend I'm not. But yeah — that's what's in there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's one step — just one — that feels real and doable to you this week? Toward that version of yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I need to talk to my unit manager. I've been dodging her for months, acting like everything's fine. But she deserves the truth. And honestly... so do I. I think that's where I start.

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm glad you came in. I know you're between classes so I don't want you to feel like you have to rush through this, but I also want to honor your time. What brought you here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, um. Okay so this is kind of hard to just... dive into. I've been drinking every day for like, years. And I always told myself it was fine because I'm an artist - like it's part of the process, it loosens me up, whatever. But last week I looked at something I made and I just... I don't know. Something was wrong with it. With me, maybe. And I got scared enough to actually make this appointment so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something in that piece scared you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It looked like noise. Not interesting noise - just... nothing. And I kept thinking maybe I just had too much before I painted it, so I had a glass of wine while I looked at it and it felt a little better and I was like, okay, crisis averted. But then the next morning I looked again and it was still bad. So. I don't know, maybe I'm overreacting. My work goes through phases.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about the work before - what it used to feel like to make something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It felt... alive. Like the stuff had something in it that was actually me. I'd feel something really intensely and I'd go make something and it would just come out. Now I drink and I wait for that and it doesn't - it doesn't come. Or it comes out wrong. And I keep drinking more thinking I just need to get there and I just... I'm starting to wonder if I broke something in myself. Like permanently.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're grieving something. The work used to feel like it was connected to something real inside you, and now it feels like that connection has gone quiet. And you're not sure if you can get back to it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. God, yeah. I've been doing this since I was twenty-two - the drinking-to-create thing. It's not like I'm some falling-down drunk. I teach, I have shows, I'm functional. But somewhere it just... shifted. And I don't know when. I wasn't paying attention and then suddenly the thing I trusted completely just wasn't working anymore and I don't - I don't know what to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real courage to sit with that question instead of just reaching for another answer. You could have had another drink. Instead you made this appointment.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I mean... yeah. I think I've known for a while that something was off but I didn't want to look at it directly. Because if the alcohol isn't helping the art anymore then - then what is it doing? Like what have I been doing to myself? That's... that's a question I don't really want the answer to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think the answer is?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Numbing me. Probably. I tell myself it's freeing me up but I think - I used to feel things so intensely and I'd just put them straight into the work. Now I feel kind of flat. All the time. Unless I'm drinking and even then it's not the same feeling, it's more like... less absence? I need more just to feel less. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes complete sense. So the drinking used to amplify something that was already there - the intensity, the feeling. And now it's more like it fills a space where feeling used to live.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I really don't like that but yes. I've been using it as a substitute for something I used to have naturally. That's - god, that's a depressing thing to realize sitting in a wellness center between my ten and my two. But yeah. That's what's happening.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I try to pull together what I'm hearing? You came in because something in your own work scared you - enough to actually show up here. You built your whole creative identity around this idea that drinking opens you up, and for a long time maybe it did. But something shifted without you noticing, and now the art is suffering, the feeling is going flat, and underneath the fear about the work is this deeper fear that something got damaged. And you've been drinking more trying to get back to something that keeps moving further away.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that it sounds so... clear. Like of course that's what's happening, why couldn't I see that. I think I've been so terrified that I can't make anything real without drinking that I never actually tested it. Not seriously. Not since I was like nineteen, twenty. What if I'm just not - what if there's nothing there without it?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to you if you found out there was?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It would mean I'm still in there somewhere. Like the drinking took something from me but not everything. That what I'm looking for isn't - it's not in a bottle, it's just... quieter than I remember it being. And I'd have to learn to hear it again. I'd have to slow down enough to hear it. I think that scares me too but in a different way. Like a better way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just described your own creative voice as something quiet you'd have to learn to hear again. That's not someone who's lost it. That's someone who knows exactly where to look.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think... I want to try. I'm not saying I'm quitting tomorrow or making some big announcement or whatever. But I want to try to make something sober. Just once, actually try, not just tell myself I can't. That feels like more than I walked in here with.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — I know you've got a tight window, so I won't waste your time. I'm glad you actually made it. What brings you in today, from your perspective?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My boss basically made me. There was, uh... an incident at work and HR said I had to come talk to someone or else. So here I am. I don't really think I need to be here, just so we're clear.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your boss sent you, and you're not convinced this is necessary.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. I mean — look, I've been going through a lot lately. My wife — my ex-wife — she decided four months ago that twenty-two years just wasn't enough for her. So yeah, I've been drinking a little more than usual. That's not a crime last time I checked.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years — that's a significant piece of your life. What's been the hardest part of all this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Everything? She gets to keep the house, she gets the kids most of the time, and I'm living in some apartment that smells like the last guy's dog. And now everyone at work is acting like I've got some big problem because I showed up a little off one morning. One morning.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the drinking's become a way to get through a lot of loss hitting all at once — your marriage, your home, your daily time with your kids.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it — I mean... I guess. I'm not like, sitting in the dark crying or whatever. I'm functional. I go to work, I pay my bills. It's just some nights are... I don't know. Long.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The nights are long. Tell me more about that — what do those nights actually look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get home and it's just... quiet. Used to come home and there'd be the kids doing homework, or arguing, or my daughter on the phone with her friends. Now it's nothing. So I'll have a few drinks, watch TV, fall asleep on the couch. Wake up and do it again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's real grief. Losing the sound of your own home.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I guess it is. I hadn't really — I don't know, I've been more angry about all of it than sad, if that makes sense. But yeah. The quiet is... it's hard.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up today. Even frustrated about it, even pressed for time — you walked in that door. That says something about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I didn't really have a choice.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Maybe not. But I'm curious — if things keep going on this track, the drinking, the situation at work... what do you see happening with your relationship with your kids?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... I don't want to think about that. My kids are — they're everything. My son's fifteen, my daughter's twelve. I don't want them to see me as... I don't want to be that guy. The dad they have to worry about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull this together. You didn't choose to be here today, but you came anyway. You've been carrying a lot — the end of a long marriage, losing daily life with your kids, a job situation that's now on the line. The drinking has helped you get through the nights, but you're starting to see it might be costing you something you really don't want to lose.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... When you put it like that. Yeah. I think I've been telling myself I've got it handled. I don't know if that's — I don't know. Maybe it's not as handled as I thought.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would 'handling it' look like to you — in a way that actually works?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Something different than what I'm doing now. I want to be... I want my kids to be proud of me. That's — yeah. That's what I want.

client_context: A 50-year-old who was sober for 3 years but relapsed after a sudden job loss. Feels deep shame and hopelessness. Has been to AA before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you today, Robert. It's been a couple weeks since we last met — how have things been going since then?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Not great. I mean, I'm here, so... that's something, right? But it's been rough. Real rough. I don't even know where to start.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something's been weighing on you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Sandra's barely talking to me. She said what she said — that she'd leave — and I... part of me is furious about it, like, I'm already feeling like garbage and now she's threatening me on top of it. And then part of me is just... what's the point, you know? If she's already got one foot out the door.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say 'what's the point' — what are you referring to? The sessions, getting sober again... all of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: All of it. I mean, I was sober for three years. THREE years. And then I lose my job — which wasn't even my fault, they laid off half the damn department — and suddenly I'm the villain? I slip once and the whole world acts like I never changed at all. That's — I'm sorry, that makes me angry.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three years of hard work, and it feels like none of that counts anymore.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Like it just... evaporated. One bad month and I'm back to square one, at least that's how everyone's treating me. Sandra, my brother, even my AA sponsor hasn't called back. So yeah. I'm a little pissed off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes sense you'd feel that way — losing your job, feeling unsupported right when things got hardest. That's a lot to absorb at once. And I hear the anger. I want to sit with that for a second and ask you something, if that's okay — when you picture six months from now, what worries you most?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Losing her. Sandra. I know I act like I'm mad at her but I've been with that woman for twenty-two years. If she actually leaves... I don't know who I am without her. That scares me more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She's not just your wife — she's part of who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, she is. And the drinking — I know it scared her. She's seen me at my worst, before I got sober the first time. I think she thought we were past it. We both did. And now I can see it in her eyes when she looks at me — like she's bracing herself. Like she's just waiting for it to get worse again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm following you, because I want to make sure I understand. You lost your job — something that wasn't in your control — and that knocked you down hard, and you relapsed. Once, after three solid years. And now you're watching Sandra pull away, feeling let down by people who were supposed to be there for you, and underneath all that anger, what's really there is fear. Fear of losing her. Does that capture it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... yeah. Yeah, that's — when you say it like that it's a lot. It's a lot to hear out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It is a lot. And you're still here — you showed up today. What does that tell you about yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know. Maybe that I actually want to fix this? I mean, nobody dragged me here. Sandra didn't drive me — I drove myself. And I know what I need to do, I know it, I've done the program before. I just let myself get isolated after the layoff and that's — that's when it all fell apart. I stopped reaching out and started drinking instead.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You drove yourself here. You know what it took to get through three years. And you've just identified exactly what went sideways — the isolation. That's not nothing, Robert. That's clarity.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I used to call my sponsor every week. Every single week. And then when I got laid off I just... I was ashamed, I didn't want to tell anyone, so I stopped calling. And, like, I can hear how dumb that sounds now. I know that's exactly backwards from what I should've done. God.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So knowing all of that — what would a first step look like for you this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I just need to call him. My sponsor. Even if it's awkward, even if he's disappointed. And... go back to a meeting. I haven't been since February. I think Sandra needs to see me actually doing the work, not just talking about it. Honestly, I think I need to see it too.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for joining today. I know this probably wasn't exactly on your to-do list. I don't want to assume anything about why you're here or what you're thinking — so I'd rather just hear it from you. What's your take on all of this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My take? My take is that this is completely insane. I had one bad morning at work and now I'm in — like, therapy? Over what? I'm 21. I'm in college. This is what we do. My boss completely overreacted and now everyone's acting like I'm some kind of... I don't even know. It's ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the whole thing feels wildly out of proportion. Like one incident got blown up into something way bigger than it deserved to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. And it's not just my boss — my friends did this whole... intervention thing. Which, okay, that was honestly insulting. My mom was crying. My mom. Over me going out on the weekends like every other person my age does. You know how many people I know who drink way more than me? Like, I'm not even close to being the worst one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The people closest to you are reacting in a pretty big way — your friends, your mom — and you're sitting here feeling like none of them are seeing it clearly. That's a frustrating place to be. Can I ask, what does a typical weekend actually look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Normal stuff. Go out Thursday, Friday, Saturday — usually bars or parties, depends on the week. Sometimes Sunday if there's like a game or whatever. I don't know, it's college. You go out, you drink, you have fun. It's literally what everyone does. I don't understand why I have to justify that to anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thursday through Sunday most weeks. And when you're out, what does drinking look like on a night like that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, like... a lot, I guess? But that's the point. You pre-game, you go out, you keep drinking. It's not like I'm doing it alone in my room or something, it's social. There's a difference. And I'm not blacking out every time or whatever. Most times. Sometimes it gets a little — but that's just... that happens. That's not a crisis.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing so far, just to make sure I've got it right. You're here because of something that happened at work — we haven't gotten into that yet. On top of that, your friends staged an intervention, your mom got emotional, and from where you're standing all of it feels completely disproportionate. You see your drinking as normal for your age, social, nothing that puts you in a different category from anyone else around you. And being in this room — or I guess, on this call — feels unfair.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. That's... yeah, that's it. I'm glad someone can at least say it back without making it sound like I'm some kind of addict. Because I'm not.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm not here to put a label on you. That's genuinely not what this is. But I do want to understand the full picture — and we've been kind of dancing around the work incident. What actually happened that day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... I mean, it was a rough weekend. I didn't sleep much and I went in Monday and I guess I — someone said something about smelling it on me and I, um... I maybe shouldn't have gone in that day. But I needed the shift. And yeah, my manager pulled me aside and it was — look, it wasn't great. But one time doesn't make you an alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like part of you already knew, going in that morning, that something was off.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... maybe. I don't know. I thought I was fine. I thought — look, I've done it before and it's been okay. That day was just bad timing. But I know what I'm doing, okay? I'm not out of control. I can stop whenever. I just... don't want to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've said a few times that you know what you're doing — and I actually believe that part of you really does pay attention. You're not someone who just floats through life without thinking. So I want to ask you something, and you don't have to answer if you're not ready. What would it mean to you — not to anyone else, just to you — if some of what the people around you are seeing... had even a little bit of truth to it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... um. That's kind of a heavy question. I don't — I guess I'd be scared. Like genuinely scared. Because my uncle, he... he had a real problem. And it took everything from him. His marriage, his job — I watched that growing up and I swore that wasn't going to be me. So I don't... I can't be that. That's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying that picture of your uncle for a long time. And somewhere in the back of your mind, there's a line you don't want to cross — and the fact that you even know that line exists says something important about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean, I still don't think I'm — I don't think I'm there. I really don't. But maybe... I don't know. Maybe everyone around me isn't completely wrong. Like maybe there's something worth looking at. I'm not saying I have a problem, I'm just saying... I don't know. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect something back to you, because I think it matters. You came into this conversation angry — and that made complete sense. This was forced, it felt unfair, and you were ready to fight it. And somewhere in the last twenty minutes, something shifted. You're not ready to call it anything, and that's fine — I'm not asking you to. But there's a part of you that's willing to look honestly, because you already know what it looks like when it gets bad, and you don't want that for yourself. That's not nothing. That's actually a lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I'm still not — I don't think I need like, rehab or anything dramatic. But I guess I can keep doing this. Talking. See what comes up. I don't want to be my uncle. That's real.
